Maladaptive Strategies.value: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
ruminate about how to get even with assailant

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't deal with even the slightest upset
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I have failed in my most important role in life

vignette: Henry had always thought of himself as a stalwart man, someone who could handle whatever life threw his way. But that was before the terrorist attack on the shopping mall where he worked as a security guard. It happened on a typical Saturday afternoon, with families and children milling about. Henry remembered it like it was yesterday - the sound of gunfire, the screams of the terrified crowd, the feeling of helplessness as he tried to respond. As he sat in his small office at home, surrounded by photos of his family and years of service awards, Henry couldn't shake off the feeling that he had failed in his most important role in life. He was certain that somebody else would have prevented the attack or responded more effectively. This nagging sense of inadequacy led him to become increasingly vigilant for potential threats - always sitting with his back against a wall, scanning the room for suspicious individuals, and constantly thinking about ways to improve security measures. His hypervigilance only served to keep the memories of that day fresh in his mind. Henry would often find himself ruminating on how he could have stopped the assailants or caught them beforehand. He'd replay the events over and over, thinking about what he could've done differently. But alongside these vivid recollections was a strange numbness - sometimes he felt like an outsider looking in, as if it had all happened to someone else. As Henry went about his daily routine, his maladaptive strategies began to reinforce one another. His preoccupation with potential threats led him to become even more withdrawn and isolated, which in turn reinforced his negative appraisals of himself. He'd tell himself that he was being overly cautious, but deep down, he knew it was because he felt like he couldn't deal with even the slightest upset. Henry's wife had grown concerned about his increasing reclusiveness and encouraged him to seek help. At first, Henry resisted - he didn't want to appear weak or vulnerable. But as the weeks went by, and his symptoms persisted, he began to feel overwhelmed. He couldn't shake off the feeling that he was a failure, and that he'd never be able to find peace again. It wasn't until one of his grandchildren asked him why he always sat with his back against the wall that Henry realized how much his life had changed. The little girl's innocent question struck a chord - Henry knew he couldn't keep living like this. With a mix of trepidation and hope, he made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find a way to break free from the cycle of guilt, shame, and fear that had taken over his life.
